title: At the market: counting and haggling
title_target: នៅផ្សារ — neuw phsaa
goal: Buy things, count them with the right classifier, and haggle — while discovering that Khmer counts objects in a very different order from English.
bekal: count things in the order noun–number–classifier
use the ten classifiers that actually matter
haggle with ចុះថ្លៃបន្តិចបានទេ?
point things out with នេះ and នោះ

dialogs.title: កិច្ចសន្ទនា — Psar Chas, seven in the morning
dialogs.intro: Sreymom takes Ani to the old market. Notice the order every time something is counted: **the thing first, then the number, then the classifier** — "mango five fruit" instead of "five mangoes". This is where English speakers have to rewire a habit.

lines.speaker: ស្រីមុំ:
lines.text: [បង|baang] [ចង់|chang] [ទិញ|teñ] [អ្វី|'wey] [ចាស|chaah]?
lines.id: What do you want to buy?

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [ខ្ញុំ|khnyom] [ចង់|chang] [ទិញ|teñ] [ផ្លែឈើ|phlae-chheu] [និង|neng] [ត្រី|trey] [ចាស|chaah]។
lines.id: I want to buy fruit and fish.
lines.literal: I — want — buy — fruit-tree — and — fish — yes(f).

lines.speaker: អ្នកលក់:
lines.text: [ស្វាយ|swaay] [ថ្មី|thmey] [ចាស|chaah]! [ផ្អែម|ph'aem] [ណាស់|nah]។

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [ស្វាយ|swaay] [ប្រាំ|pram] [ផ្លែ|phlae] [ថ្លៃ|thlay] [ប៉ុន្មាន|pon-maan] [ចាស|chaah]?
lines.literal: mango — five — fruit — price — how-much — yes(f)?

lines.speaker: អ្នកលក់:
lines.text: [មួយ|muèy] [ម៉ឺន|meun] [រៀល|riel] [ចាស|chaah]។

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [ថ្លៃ|thlay] [ណាស់|nah]! [ចុះថ្លៃ|choh-thlay] [បន្តិច|ban-tech] [បាន|baan] [ទេ|té] [ចាស|chaah]?
lines.id: That's very expensive! Can you come down a little?
lines.literal: expensive — very! lower-price — a-little — can — (question) — yes(f)?

lines.speaker: អ្នកលក់:
lines.text: [ប្រាំបី|pram-bey] [ពាន់|poan] [ចុះ|choh]។ [ចុងក្រោយ|chong-kraoy] [ហើយ|haeuy] [ចាស|chaah]។
lines.id: Eight thousand, then. That's my last price.
lines.literal: five-three — thousand — go-down. end-last — already — yes(f).

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [បាន|baan] [ចាស|chaah]។ [ចុះ|choh] [ត្រី|trey] [នេះ|nih]?

lines.speaker: អ្នកលក់:
lines.text: [ត្រី|trey] [ពីរ|pii] [ក្បាល|kbaal] [ដប់ពីរ|dop-pii] [ពាន់|poan] [ចាស|chaah]។
lines.literal: fish — two — head — ten-two — thousand — yes(f).

lines.speaker: ស្រីមុំ:
lines.text: [បង|baang]! [យក|yòòk] [ត្រី|trey] [នោះ|nuh] [ល្អ|l'aa] [ជាង|chièng]។ [ធំ|thum] [ជាង|chièng]។
lines.id: Bong! Take that fish, it's better. It's bigger.
lines.literal: older-sibling! take — fish — that — good — more. big — more.

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [អញ្ចឹង|'añ-cheung] [យក|yòòk] [ត្រី|trey] [នោះ|nuh] [ពីរ|pii] [ក្បាល|kbaal] [ចាស|chaah]។ [ទាំងអស់|teang-'ah] [ប៉ុន្មាន|pon-maan]?
lines.id: In that case I'll take two of those. How much altogether?
lines.literal: like-that — take — fish — that — two — head — yes(f). all — how-much?

lines.speaker: អ្នកលក់:
lines.text: [ម្ភៃ|m-phey] [ពាន់|poan] [ចាស|chaah]។ [ថង់|thang] [មួយ|muèy] [ឬ|reu] [ពីរ|pii]?
lines.id: Twenty thousand. One bag or two?
lines.literal: twenty — thousand — yes(f). bag — one — or — two?

lines.speaker: អានី:
lines.text: [មួយ|muèy] [ថង់|thang] [គ្រប់គ្រាន់|krup-kroan] [ចាស|chaah]។ [អរគុណ|'aa-kun]!
lines.id: One bag is enough. Thank you!

grammars.title: Counting things: noun first, number second
body: Khmer counts in the order **noun – number – classifier**. English has a faint echo of the classifier in "two *head* of cattle" or "three *sheets* of paper", but Khmer uses one with almost every noun — and puts it after the number, with the noun at the very front.

head: Khmer
Say it
Literally
English
rows: ស្វាយ ប្រាំ ផ្លែ
ត្រី ពីរ ក្បាល
សិស្ស ដប់ នាក់
តែ មួយ កែវ
ផ្ទះ បី ខ្នង

after: ⚠️ This is the reverse of English (*five mangoes*). The number never goes in front of the noun. Say the thing first, as if pointing at it, then count it: "mangoes — five of them".

If you forget the classifier: **just repeat the noun** — ថ្ងៃ បី ថ្ងៃ ("day three day") is correct and common. Or **leave it out altogether** — ស្វាយ ប្រាំ sounds casual but is never wrong. Khmer is far more relaxed about this than Thai.

grammars.title: នេះ and នោះ — pointing while you shop
body: Demonstratives stand **after** the noun: "fish this" = this fish. Nothing changes for the plural.

head: Khmer
Say it
Meaning
rows: ស្វាយទាំងនេះ

after: At the market, pointing with your index finger is considered a bit rude. Cambodians point with **the whole hand, palm open and facing up**, or simply with the chin and a glance. Saying យកមួយនេះ while opening your palm is more than enough.

grammars.title: Haggling: the unwritten rules of Psar Chas
body: Haggling at a traditional Cambodian market is not a fight but an expected conversation. Accepting the first price actually makes the vendor feel you have no interest in chatting.

head: English
Khmer
Say it
rows: Can you come down a little?
ចុះថ្លៃបន្តិចបានទេ?
ចុងក្រោយប៉ុន្មាន?
អញ្ចឹង ខ្ញុំយក
លើកក្រោយចុះ

after: **Offer about three quarters of the first price**, not half. Offering half — a habit of some tourists — is seen as not serious and often ends the conversation.

⚠️ **Don't haggle in shops with price tags, at food stalls, or in supermarkets.** Haggling only applies at traditional markets and with tuk-tuks. Haggling over the price of a bowl of noodles sounds like haggling over your electricity bill.
And most important: **smile**. Haggling with a straight face reads as anger. The final sentence that closes a deal is almost always said with a little laugh.

blocks.text: ⚠️ Adjectives stand **after** the noun — the reverse of English: ស្វាយធំ = "mango big", ថង់ក្រហម = "bag red". And as unit 14 will explain in full, Khmer adjectives are really **verbs** — so ស្វាយធំ can also mean "the mango is big" as a complete sentence, with no "is" needed.
